inferences: A band whose raised and cut takes disagree about its centre by more than the spread the other seven show, which would mean the eight are not fixed sections but something whose position moves with its gain. A width setting whose half-gain span differs from the equaliser's at the four entries the band set contains by more than the twelfth of an octave the reading steps in. A gain byte answering outside 52 to 76.

A byte a page prints `Post Gain` against `0/+6/+12/+18` is four fixed steps of six decibels, and it stands after the stage it is named for. Both of the two types the document prints the parameter against were measured, three held states between them and nine steps in all, mean 5.999 decibels over a spread of 0.09. That it is after rather than in front of the stage is the one of the two that a level alone cannot say, and it is read from the set taken where the limiter is taking thirty decibels off: the steps there are 6.03, 6.02 and 5.96 decibels, which a gain written in front of a stage removing that much could not return.

A byte printed `D> 0E - D 0<E` is two multipliers, each of them the byte's distance from a corner divided by fifty, truncated onto a grid of a hundred and twenty-eight and clamped at both ends -- and the two are offset so that they meet at full rather than crossing. The half that goes past the effect holds at its dry-end level for every setting up to and including 64, leaves it at 65, and is at nothing from 114 on. Read every count over both corners, thirty-two settings land within a sixth of a step of `min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128)` on the ramp and within half a step anywhere, and each of the three numbers in it is pinned by the reading: a quarter of a count on the width costs six times the residual, rounding instead of truncating costs seven times it, and the multipliers sit a twelfth of a step from the grid's entries where a number on no grid would sit a quarter of one away. Read in the window the return arrives in, the effect's own half rises for the last time at 64 and holds from 65, ten times what the takes repeat either way, so it is the direct half reflected through 128 rather than through 127: `min(1, floor((n - 14) * 128 / 50) / 128)`, whose corner and the direct half's sum to 128, and which meets the direct half at full at exactly 64. That half is read on two of the three types and carried by a shape rather than a threshold: truncation makes the four steps over the corner uneven, and reflected through 128 they are predicted at 0.220, 0.144, 0.211 and 0.206 of a decibel and read within 0.010 of that on one type and 0.031 on the other, where reflecting through 127 is out by 0.200 and 0.175. So the middle of the byte carries both halves at once and stands three decibels over either end, which is the opposite sign to a crossfade and not flat. Both ends reach true nothing: the direct window at the effect end falls to 1.1 decibels over the same take's own lead, which is the interface and not the unit. The law was found on one type at one count and holds on the two others, read at eight counts on a different day, to seven tenths of a step.

A byte printed `L63 - 0 - R63` is one multiplier a side, the same pair on types whose front halves have nothing in common, and what stops it twenty-five decibels short of silence is not the multiplier. Read one band at a time the two channels separate by 33.7 decibels more in some bands than in others at the ends of the sweep and alike in all of them through the middle, against the same pair of channels with the effect taken out of the path separating alike everywhere to 0.1 of a decibel. A pair of multipliers has no frequency in it and cannot do that. Allow one term added after the pan and nineteen settings of twenty bands come back as one multiplier each, over 342 readings to a median of 0.17 decibels -- agreeing with the broadband balance to a tenth through the middle of the sweep and departing from it by two decibels at the last byte, which is where the broadband reading was reading the added term. The table's two sides are one table read in opposite directions, 0.54 of a decibel apart at worst over 17 settings, and its centre entry sits 2.44 decibels under its end -- neither the 3.01 of a constant-power pair nor the 6.02 of a straight crossfade.

A byte the page prints identically on this multi and on the phaser returning a different profile at the settings both were read at, under the same hold and on the same band set. Or either half's level byte at nothing leaving silence, which would make the two stages a chain and make every profile here a reading of the two together.

A comb in any of the six that sits at a spacing the single type does not return, at either delay setting or on either sign of the loop. One reading off the single type's two figures by more than the width the fit reports would say the stage is named after something it is not.

A delay's damping byte is one pole inside the delay's own feedback loop, and it is the pole written the cheapest way there is: a running average, one multiply and one state, with no zero at half the rate. Inside rather than once on the way out, which is read off how a held note builds: with the byte at the position the page prints as the filter out the build is 18.3 dB and it is the same in every band, and with the filter in it falls away above a frequency that moves more than four octaves across the byte. A filter outside the loop is the same shape in both windows and cancels between them. That is not the section the same part's chorus filter byte sits on. A pole put through the bilinear transform keeps a zero at half the rate and its skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it; this one has no zero, so its skirt stops cutting and levels off -- and the profile does level off, on every one of the ten settings the run asked, at a different depth each time. Where a profile levels off names the pole outright with nothing fitted, because the depth is one minus the coefficient over one plus it. Scored through the same takes the cheap pole is sixteen times the bilinear one's median and is the only candidate of eight whose residual does not lean. And it names the clock a fourth time, by a route none of the first three used: the coefficient that puts the corner where the page prints it depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely from each setting's own skirt lands on the printed third octaves to a five-hundredth of an octave at thirty-two kilohertz and a twentieth at forty-four -- high at every setting, which is a lean and not a scatter. Read on two more types the same byte does one of two things. On the modulated delay it is the same byte doing the same thing: over ten settings and a hundred and thirteen bands the two profiles sit a median 0.045 dB apart, which is under what either run failed to repeat, and the corners agree to a fifteenth of an octave. Nothing was refitted for it -- the claim was closed on one type and reproduced on a second it had never seen. Inside the chorus-and-delay pair it is not. There the profiles sit a median 10.04 dB apart, and the shape is the thing that differs rather than the depth: on both delays the skirt is still falling at the top of the band, by 10.15 dB over the last two octaves at the byte's bottom, while in the pair it has flattened to -0.08 and sits at -24.38 dB from two kilohertz upward. Two explanations for that were tried and both are refused. It is not the run's floor: restricted to the bands where each setting's own take stands twelve decibels clear of its own silence the disagreement is still 10.04 dB. And it is not the held block meaning different things -- the delay time and the feedback on all three types are printed on one conversion column and one hex range, so the same byte is the same quantity, and what differs in the print is each type's own default. What the pair's profile is, is not read here. The claim is a claim about one slot and it now has one type it reaches and one it does not.

A delay-time byte does not scale a time and does not run a formula. It indexes a ladder of round decimal milliseconds whose step changes a few times over the byte, and every entry is then cut back to a whole step of a clock running at 32000 Hz -- which is what a delay addressed as a sample count does to a time written in milliseconds. Which ladder a slot is on is picked by the conversion column the effect list cites beside it, not by the range the page prints -- two slots print the same range and cite different columns, and they return ladders fifty milliseconds apart. On 0 - 500m the step is a tenth of a millisecond to setting fifty, then a half to sixty, then one to ninety, then ten to a hundred and sixteen, then twenty to a hundred and twenty-six; on 0 - 100m it is the same tenth to fifty and half to sixty, then one to a hundred, then two to a hundred and twenty-five; on 200m - 990m/1sec the byte starts at two hundred milliseconds and steps five to setting seventy, then ten to a hundred and fifteen, where it reaches one second; on 0m - 635m the step never changes at all -- five milliseconds from the first setting to the last; and 0m - 500m, which the page spells with an m the other five-hundred range does not have, is that range's ladder entry for entry. Four of the five reach the printed end before the byte ends and repeat it at every setting above, and the fifth reaches it at its last setting, so where a ladder stops is read off the record in both directions. The cut is not a detail of the ladder: it is what the settings at the short end actually return, and it is what decides which settings the reading brings back a tall peak for. It is also why two of the five ranges say nothing about the clock -- every entry on them is five milliseconds or more, which is already a whole step of it, so there is no setting at which the two readings differ. One slot of the five does not read its ladder from wherever it is asked. On the type whose delay glides, a setting reached from below is short of its cited column by a thousand and sixteen whole samples of the same clock, and the same setting reached from above returns that column times a hundred and twenty-seven over a hundred and twenty-eight exactly -- the same one-byte ratio every entry here carries. So the shortfall the sweep found is the sweep's own direction and not a second regime in the table, and the byte the page prints beside it as an acceleration is worth exactly half of it, from its top bit alone and from no other bit in the nibble. The ladder a column picks is the same ladder at every address that cites it. One type prints four of these rows at four addresses, three of which nothing in this class had been read at, and prints a different default against each -- 500ms, 300ms, 400ms, 200ms -- where the conversion column is one column for all four. All four return the ladder read on the type beside it, to within 0.042 ms at every setting either was asked at, against a floor of 0.0834 ms on the noisiest of them and 0.0 on the other three. So the printed default is not what picks a ladder either, which the page gives no other way to tell. A column's ladder does not change for what stands in front of the delay either. Four types that print this row put another stage before or beside it -- an enhancer, a chorus in front, a chorus beside, a flanger beside -- and every one of them returns the ladder its column was read on, to within 0.000 ms at all eight settings asked of each, on a reading quantised to 0.020833 ms. Two more print it behind a waveshaper and are not read here, for a reason that is about the reading and not about the byte.

A drive setting between 8 and 48 whose orders no input level reproduces, by more than the bar the ladder measures at that input. Or the wanted input ceasing to follow the byte's value in decibels once the ladder is extended -- the run reached thirty-six decibels of input and the law was checked over forty of drive, and a longer ladder could break it where this one could not look. Or the output level byte turning out to move the orders after all on some other type, which would make every comparison here a comparison through a gain and the whole reading an artefact of loudness.

A filter byte's corner sits on a single pole, and both filters this type's type byte selects are one pole each. The low pass falls six decibels an octave through the middle of the band and the high pass the same the other way; neither is a biquad and neither is two poles cascaded, which would be twelve. The low pass carries the zero the bilinear transform leaves at half the rate, and that is what makes a clock readable off it: the skirt bends from 5.7 decibels an octave between 800 Hz and 1.6 kHz to 10.3 between 6.4 and 12.7 kHz, which puts half the rate just above the top of the band and the rate at thirty-two kilohertz. Read at forty-four or forty-eight it is four times worse and leans. The high pass names the order and cannot name the rate: its corners are all under 500 Hz, its zero is at nothing, and the place a warp would show is its own flat passband. One corner table serves both -- at the four settings both were read the two agree to within 0.064 octaves, which is what this reading resolves.

A frequency byte does not drive a formula and does not have a hundred and twenty-eight values. Its top four bits index a table of sixteen entries, so eight settings share each entry, and the entries are the named third octaves between the two frequencies the page prints against that address -- with one that is not. On 200 - 6.3k, fifteen of the sixteen sit within 0.07 octaves of 200, 250, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1k, 1.25k, 1.6k, 2k, 2.5k, 3.15k, 4k, 5k and 6.3k, a median 0.03 and under what a twelfth-octave reading resolves. The third entry sits at 279 Hz where the series says 315, which is 0.18 octaves and two bands, and it is the only entry the reading and the series disagree about. Both mid sections return that same 279, and they return the whole of the first four entries to within 0.002 octaves of each other, so the two index one table rather than two. Read across its own eight settings the entry does not move -- 279.1, 278.7, 278.8 and 279.0 at 16, 17, 20 and 23 -- and the settings either side of it return the entries either side, so the stride is eight and the number in the table is 279.

A gain byte over a peaking section does not build the section at the gain it names. One section is stored at the top of the printed range and the byte blends it against the dry path, and a cut is that same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. The two readings agree at both ends of the window and at its centre and nowhere between, which is why nothing in this archive had noticed: at six decibels of a twelve decibel range the peak is about forty per cent narrower than the width byte asked for, and it is the width and not the height that says so -- every candidate here stands where the byte asked.

A gain byte over this type's low shelf does not build the shelf at the gain it names either, and it does not reach it the way the two mid sections of the same type are reached. One shelf is stored at the bottom of the printed range -- the full cut -- and the byte blends the dry path towards that, with a boost being the same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. In coefficients it is the same three multiply-accumulates the mid sections use, moved from the numerator to the denominator, and the two are not the same curve: the mid reading has the low shelf falling away half an octave sooner in the middle of the window than the unit does, and this one is out by a quarter of a band.

A gain byte printed -12 - +12 is decibels, one per step, offset by sixty-four. It answers over a window of twenty-five values from 52 to 76 and returns the nearest end for everything outside. And the two of them that forty-three types carry with no frequency printed beside either are this unit's equaliser's own shelf pair with the frequency byte taken away and pinned to its first printed entry.
A gain ladder with a notch switched across it, and a shelf table -- two tables under one printed name.

A modulation wave byte indexes five fixed shapes and computes nothing, and four of the five are the shapes the page names them. Read on two types that drive different quantities with the same byte -- one swinging its output's level by more than the whole of its own mean, the other swinging the balance between its channels by forty decibels -- the entry printed `Tri` returns a triangle, `Sqr` a square and `Saw1` and `Saw2` a sawtooth, each nearer the shape it is named after than any other by both of the two readings taken, on both types, 8 readings out of 8. `Saw1` and `Saw2` are one shape run two ways: no reading of magnitudes can separate them, which the two candidates sitting exactly zero apart under both scores says outright, and what separates them is that one spends nine tenths of its cycle climbing and the other one tenth. The fifth entry is not what it is printed. `Sin` carries a third harmonic of four to six hundredths where a sine has none and a triangle has a ninth, and a fifth harmonic of two thousandths where a triangle has a twenty-fifth -- so it is neither, and it is a sine made cheaply. Which cheap sine is not settled and is queued. The shape is a shape of a multiplier and not of a level: the same cycles come back clean read in amplitude and warped read in decibels, which is what a gain swung linearly does to a logarithm and not what a gain swung in decibels would do to either. Three readings stood against this and each had a run; all three ran. The five shapes are not these two types': the third place the same five names are printed returns the same five, entry for entry, no further apart than 0.0122 in any harmonic either reading carries, with both sawtooths climbing the same way round. The depth byte scales the cycle rather than reshaping it, and what looked like a shape moving with depth was the reading's own logarithm: read as a difference between two channels in decibels the third harmonic sits a median 0.0582 from the linear reading at the top of the byte and 0.0166 at a quarter of it, converging on it as the swing shrinks and the logarithm straightens. And the entry printed `Sin` is not the parabola. It is not the parabola, and it is refused from both sides at once. Rendered onto one of this unit's own takes and read back through the whole stage, the parabola returns a third harmonic of 0.0409 where the unit returns 0.0600, and a fifth of 0.0054 where the unit returns 0.0029 -- too little of the one and more than twice too much of the other, which no scaling of a candidate can fix in both directions at once. What fits is a sine carrying a small third harmonic and almost nothing above it: a sine carrying a fifteenth of its third lands 0.0038 away where the parabola lands 0.0112, 3.0 times as far. That is a description of the cycle and not a name for what makes it, and this file does not give it one.

A peaking section at half its gain coming back the width its width byte asks for. Or a cut coming back a different width from the boost of the same height. Or a setting in the middle of the window whose profile is not the blend's, at more than the one band this reading resolves.

A rate byte does not drive a formula. It indexes a printed table of whole steps of a twentieth of a hertz, and there are two such tables, told apart by the range the page prints against the address. The narrow one is 128 entries of 0.05 Hz, from 0.05 to 6.40. The wide one shares those entries as far as 5.00 Hz at setting 99, then steps by 0.10 to 7.00 at 119 and by 0.50 to 10.00 at 125 -- 126 entries, so the last two settings of the byte have no entry of their own and return the last one. One table serves every type: the same twenty-one slots across nineteen effect types answer to it with no per-type constant anywhere.

A reading at any setting of any admissible slot that is not the entry these tables give, by more than one entry. Or a wide-range slot whose bend sits somewhere other than settings 100 and 120. Or a rate row on the page carrying a printed range that is neither of the two, which would mean there is a third table this claim does not know about.

A reading at any setting of any of these slots that is not its range's ladder entry for it, by more than that setting's own resolution. Or a slot on another type one of these ranges is printed against whose ladder has different steps, which would make the printed range the wrong thing to index by. Or the same sweep on a unit whose delay is not clocked at 32000 Hz coming back with the heights split the same way, which would mean the split is not the grid.
A reading of either byte on a second unit of this model returning a different number of rungs, a different step, or the dip at a frequency that is not a quarter of this clock.

A reading of either slot that puts the output somewhere else at any setting: a change between two byte values this rule puts on one position, or no change between two it puts on neighbouring ones, judged against what the same pair of takes says a position differs from itself by. One position out of thirty-one landing elsewhere refutes it, because nothing in it was fitted to be moved.

A rotary's acceleration byte is read through its top four bits, and the sixteen entries that leaves are what the rotor's loop multiplies the difference by before shifting it. So the distance the rotor stops short of the rate entry it was aimed at is one constant divided by what the entry holds. What the entries hold is a sequence: the first ten count up, one through ten, and then they double -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight. 14 of the sixteen are readable and 12 of those land on that sequence inside what their own take told a rate apart to, with one constant over the whole table and nothing else fitted. The last one does not: it reads 168 where the doubling says 256, five times what the take resolves, and it is published as the number it is. The byte is not a shift count, which is what a four-bit acceleration invited: the distance does not halve per step of it, and the near-four between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults happen to sit in this table. The two rotors are one routine reached twice -- at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent. And the constant, 0.9768 Hz, names the clock a fifth time by a route none of the other four used: it is a rate divided by a power of two, and at thirty-two kilohertz that power is 14.9996 while at forty-four and forty-eight no integer power comes within four tenths.

A rotary's slow rate byte indexes the same printed table every other rate byte on this unit indexes -- the wide one, picked by the `0.05 - 10.0` the page prints against it, with no constant of its own anywhere in it. What the rotary adds is that the entry is where a rotor is sent and not where it ends up. Sent down, it arrives exactly -- which is measured and not inferred: the same byte written after a faster one, with no reset between, comes back on its entry where the same byte written after a reset comes back short of it. Sent up, it stops a fixed distance short: 0.245 Hz on the low rotor and 0.062 on the high, holding to a thousandth of a hertz from the corner to the top of the byte and across both places the table's own step changes. And where the distance to the entry is narrower than that, the rotor barely sets off, so five entries of the low rotor's table return one rate and the high rotor moves a fifth of an entry across the one entry of its own. The width of that flat stretch and the size of the gap are the same number, which is what separates this from a constant subtracted after a lookup: read the gap off the top of the sweep alone and it places the corner, which neither half of the fit was shown. The distance is set by the acceleration byte the page prints against each rotor, and the two rotors are one routine reached twice: at every one of nine settings of that byte the two gaps agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, so the four to one between them is the two defaults and not the two rotors. What that byte does is a claim of its own beside this one.

A rotor sent down to an entry arriving short of it as well, which would make the gap a property of the table rather than of the arrival. Or the flat stretch at the bottom of the byte turning out to be a different width from the gap, which would make them two numbers rather than one. Or the acceleration byte turning out not to move the gap at all, which would leave the gap unexplained and the reading a description rather than a mechanism.

A setting inside 52 to 76 whose gain is not the byte minus sixty-four decibels by more than a fifth of one, on a section that reads the gain rather than a flank, at more than one width. Or a type whose Low Gain profile at full boost is not the equaliser's low shelf at its first printed corner.

A setting of any of the eleven bytes whose band profile the chain cannot produce at all -- a second peak, an asymmetric one, a corner that moves with the gain applied through it. Or a byte turning out to answer at values the tables here say are repeats: the widths at 5 and above, the centres between multiples of eight, the gains outside 52 to 76.

A setting of either byte returning a step that is not six decibels by more than the run's own repeats, or a held state of either type in which the step is smaller than six because the stage in front of it has taken some of it. Either would say the byte is not four fixed steps, or is not where this claim puts it.

A setting of either filter whose skirt runs at a slope no whole number of poles gives, or a low pass whose skirt is still at six decibels an octave at the top of the band, which would put half the rate outside it. Or the same sweep on a corner byte of another type coming back at twelve, which would make the section this type's and not the part's.

A setting of the manual byte whose profile has a number of cancellations no single section count explains, or notches whose positions in the tangent of frequency are not fixed multiples of one corner. Either would say the sections do not share a corner, which is the whole of this structure. A rate other than thirty-two kilohertz fitting better once the profile can be read above sixteen would refute the rate without touching the section count.

A setting of the swept byte whose period comes back at the step byte's printed rate rather than at its own, with the step byte running at a rate the swept byte does not exceed. Or modulation at any setting of the swept byte with the step byte at the bottom of its table: a clock that has stopped cannot leave a stage moving, and the partial level swing there is the bypassed take's.

A setting of this byte on any of these types whose direct window lands more than one step of the grid from `min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128)` times its own reading at the dry end. In particular any reading between 56 and 64 that is not level with the reading at 0, any reading between 114 and 127 that has not gone to the take's own lead, or a run of settings on the ramp whose steps do not alternate between two sizes -- a straight line that is not truncated steps evenly. On the effect's own half, a late window that does not rise from 63 to 64, or that rises again after 64, on any type whose return arrives clear of the note.

A setting of this byte on any of these types whose two channels land somewhere the published table does not put them, by more than the spread three voices produce at that setting. Or a band of one setting at which the two channels separate by what the recovered multiplier says while another band of the same setting does not, which is the one thing the added term is not allowed to do -- it is a term, not a filter on the pan. Or the same byte on a fourth type returning a different pair: two of the three here agree to 0.11 dB at every setting and the third to 0.93, so a type disagreeing by a decibel would say the tail is not one structure after all.

A setting of this byte that raised the profile without putting a resonance between the notches, or one that moved a notch, either of which would make the byte something other than a loop gain. Or the top band coming back where an instantaneous loop puts it on a second run, which would take the sample of delay away. Or the shortfall at the bottom of the band turning out not to follow the loop gain, which would move the high pass out of the return path.

A setting of this byte whose skirt went on cutting past its corner instead of levelling off, which would put the bilinear zero back. Or the depth it levels off at failing to follow the corner the page prints, which is the one thing about this section that is fixed rather than fitted. Or the same sweep on another type's damping byte coming back bilinear, which would make the section this slot's rather than the part's damping routine.

A setting whose multiplier sits a third of a step or more from the 1/127 grid while its take is well clear of the chain's silence, which no admitted setting does -- the worst is 0.24 of a step at setting 122, where one step is 0.068 decibels and the run resolves 0.01. Or another denominator scanned over the same settings coming closer, which none of the sixty-one does by a factor of ten. Or a level byte on another type returning multipliers that sit on no grid at all, which would make this a property of one effect rather than of how a gain is stored.

A shelf at half its gain falling away where the width of the stored full-scale boost would put it, or where the section built at that gain would. Or a boost whose shape is not its cut's, at more than the one band this reading resolves. Or the same reading on another type's shelf coming back the mid sections' way.

A sixth setting of the byte returning a sixth shape, which would make this a range rather than a table of five. Or any of the four named entries coming back as something else on a third type, by more than the two types here differ from each other. Or the harmonics moving with the depth byte, which would mean the cycles reported are one point of a surface and the table is not a table of shapes at all.

A slot whose page prints a list of states, asked from one of them at a value outside the list, coming back audible. Cheapest on a slot that powers up in a state it is not being written from: on this unit that is any of the four asked here at nought against two, and the same pair on a printed list longer than two would extend it further. It would also be refuted by a slot where the store does not read back what was written, because then the refusal is the store's and this claim is about the wrong thing.

A state of the mode byte whose distance is not the ratio the five lengths stand in, by more than four takes of that state land apart. Every state is now bounded at 0.021 ms, which is the reading's own grid step, so any of the five can refute this and the fifth is no longer the one that cannot.

A take at a setting below 64 that returns the fast byte's rate, or one at or above it that returns the slow byte's. Either would mean the turnover is not where this puts it, and each of the thirteen settings asked was a place that could have happened. Also by the fast byte returning something that is not the printed table: it was read at ten settings and no entry was fitted, so any of the ten could have refused.

A third byte on this column returning corners that are not these -- the hum generator's low pass at 40 03 0F is printed on it and has not been read, and the reason it has not is that a hum is a line spectrum whose twelfth-octave profile is a reading of where its harmonics are rather than of a filter. A skirt anywhere on this column running at twelve decibels an octave would take the order with it. And a note played through this type with 40 03 05 swept, returning nothing, would take the structural half of this back: the claim is that the generators are summed after that filter, which requires it to be somewhere.

A tone control on a third type whose corners are not these, which would make the pair the type's rather than the part's. Or either shelf read with a band set reaching past where it settles and coming back at twelve decibels an octave.

A width byte does not hold the number the page prints against it. It indexes five entries and they are the printed figures halved -- 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 -- put into the section as the width its bandwidth is defined by at the half-gain points, which is the form the era's filter arithmetic is written in. Settings past the fifth return what the first returns, which on this slot is also the entry it powers up in, so the two cannot be told apart from these takes. A fourth type carrying the same printed table tells them apart by disagreeing with both: its byte powers up at the third entry and everything past the fifth returns the fifth, so which entry a byte outside the printed steps comes back at is a property of the slot and not of the table. The five entries do not depend on where the peak is: the same table answers with the centre at the bottom of its own table and with it in the middle, and the two mid sections of the type answer alike.

A width byte read at the narrowest setting, at a centre the frequency table places in its own band, coming back at the printed figure rather than half of it. Or the same setting returning two different widths at two centres, which would make the entries coefficient sets stored per centre and not a table. Or a setting past the fifth returning anything the first five do not.

An azimuth byte does not scale an angle and does not have 128 values. Two is added to it, the result is shifted right two places, the centre is taken off, and what is left is stopped at 15 either way -- so the byte reaches 31 positions 12 degrees apart, from L180 through 0 to R180. The added two is the rounding of a divide by four and nothing else: without it every position would sit a byte off the one the page prints. Twenty nine of the positions are 4 byte values wide and the two poles are 6, which is not a widening of those positions but the clamp taking the two values at each end of the byte the shift would have carried past them. The two poles are one place: half a turn to the left is half a turn to the right, and the page writes that into both cells rather than leaving it to be noticed.

An effect parameter whose page prints a list of states takes no byte that is not one of them, and what it does instead is nothing: the parameter goes on sounding the state it was already in. The store is not what refuses -- it keeps every seven-bit value and reads it back, 02 for a write of 02 -- so whatever drops the value sits between the store and the sound. Read on five two-state slots across three of the effect map's high bytes, where nought against one is audible by 11.74 to 15.49 dB of level and one against two, one against 127 and nought against two are all null -- fifteen pairs whose two settings sit between 2.94 dB under and 0.27 dB over the yardstick those settings' own repeats set, against the 6 dB a verdict here has to clear, and none of which moves the level by more than 0.02 dB. The last of those three pairs is the one that decides it: four of the five slots power up in the second state, so a byte that reached the state they power up in would have made nought against two as loud as nought against one. Three printed lists of different lengths agree -- a two-state corner holds at the 1 it had, a three-state amp table and a five-state width both hold at the 0 they had. Those three were all asked on slots that power up at the first entry, where holding what they had and folding to the first are one number, so every length this page prints was then asked again on a slot that powers up inside its own list: a three-state filter selector and a four-state amp table that power up at 1, and a five-state width inside a multi-effect that powers up at 2. Each was asked one past its top three times over -- standing at nought, standing at the value it powers up in, and standing at its last printed state -- and the three readings that a longer list leaves standing each predict a different two of those three to be audible. All nine are null, between 3.79 dB under and 0.87 dB over the yardstick their own settings' repeats set, while the nine in-range pairs of the same three slots are audible by 16.08 to 38.17 dB over theirs. None of the three moves again further up: nought against 127 and the last printed state against 127 are null on each. Eight of the fifty-four slots printed `00/01` now carry it, over eight types including a delay line, a distortion and three guitar multi-effects, each audible at nought against one by 25.66 dB or more and null at nought against two. And the four slots the page prints `00/7F` are not a longer or shorter case of this but a different thing entirely: each was swept over the whole byte with the type reloaded before every take, so what comes back is a function of the byte alone -- the slow rotor from nought to 63 and the fast one from 64 to 127 -- while a slot printed `00/01` returns two different states for the one byte 2 depending on which state it was standing in. No map from a byte to a state does both.

An entry read in a fourth place returning a profile that is not the one the other three return, by more than the spacing between two entries of the table. Or the ratio between two entries moving with the drive byte, which would put the filter before the nonlinearity after all and make the four profiles a reading of one drive amount rather than a table. Or the switch turning out to do something other than put the filter in the path -- if its Off position were a fifth response rather than no response, the whole reading of entry 0 as a narrow box would go with it.

An insertion effect's output level byte is a multiplier stored as a whole number over a hundred and twenty-seven, and that multiplier is not the byte. Every one of the hundred and twenty-five settings the run could read returns a gain that sits on the 1/127 grid: a median 0.0225 of a step away, against 0.2185 for the next best denominator of the sixty-one asked and 0.25 for a number that sat on no grid at all. What the entries are is a curve and not a formula -- the multiplier is three quarters of the byte over the bottom quarter of the range and rises to the byte itself at the top, and no law in the catalogue crosses that. The byte read straight as the multiplier is out by a median 1.61 decibels and by 3.53 at setting 9.

Any setting whose measured rate is not `|r - 1|` over a window the mode byte alone decides. Two shapes of that: a coarse sweep returning one rate rather than one length, which is what a clock of the stage's own would give and is what the eighteenfold sweep was made to look for; or a mode byte that moves the rate at a fixed shift by anything other than the ratio it moves it by at a different shift, which is what a mode byte selecting something other than a length would give. Separately, a rate at unison. The claim says the splice stops there, so a line at byte 64 that is not the line the bypassed voice carries refutes it outright.

Each cited record says what one slot did at the settings it was asked at. None of them says what happens to a value the page has no state for, because each on its own has at least two readings that fit it: the runs that swept past a printed list all reset and reloaded the type between settings, which put the parameter's loaded value and its standing value in the same place, and the one slot anybody had looked at past its list powers up at 0, where folding to the first state, returning the loaded value and keeping the current one are three names for the same number. What is added is the pair that pulls them apart -- nought against two, written in that order with nothing reset in between, on slots that power up at 1 -- and the reading of all of them together as one rule rather than as a habit of one type. Round two adds the shape that lets one slot answer alone. A list of more than two states has three predecessors worth standing in -- nought, the value the type loads, and the last printed state -- and asking one past the top from each of them separates keeping the current state from returning the loaded value, from folding to the first, and from clamping to the last, without putting two slots side by side to do it. Round three closes the last list length the page prints and takes the reading to eight slots over eight types, and it reads a refutation out of records that were already published: the two spellings cannot be one map from the byte to a state, because one of them is such a map and the other is not.

Each record says what one address of one type held at power on, and each says in as many words that the printed range beside it is evidence about a page rather than about the unit. The page says what a parameter's default is, in the parameter's own units, and does not say which byte that is. Neither says the two agree, and turning one into the other needs a third table -- the conversion grid, for every parameter whose byte does not carry its setting. This file is where the three are joined.

Each record says what one cycle of one setting's modulator looks like, as a curve and as harmonics, and puts no name on it. What is read out of them here is which of five named shapes each cycle is -- which is a comparison against a page and against four analytic shapes, neither of which is in either record -- and that the five are one table because two types driving different quantities return them.

Each record says what one slot's byte did at the settings it was asked at, and each says in as many words that no law, no table and no verdict is in it and that the printed range beside it is evidence about a page rather than about the unit. This file is where the two are joined: that the readings of twenty-one slots are one table read through nineteen effects, that the printed pair picks which of two, and that the entries are what they are. None of that is in any record, and no rerun of a stage would produce it.

Each record says what one type's pre-filter byte does to a band profile. What is read out of the pair is that the two profiles are the same profile -- a comparison between records, made against a third figure neither record states, which is what one step of the swept byte is worth under the same reading.

Each record says what the level was at each setting of the threshold byte under one state of the ratio byte. What is read out of them here is what no one of them holds: that the four together are not four multipliers of one quantity. The scale of the threshold byte in decibels is read off the state that is linear in it, the other three are then held against that scale, and the departure is a comparison across four records. The ladder adds the second thing none of the sweeps can say, because the byte it would have to be said with has run out of range.

Each record says which band the deviation was largest in at each setting it was asked at, where a curve fitted over the whole feature puts its top, and says in as many words that no filter, no corner and no order is in it. Nothing in any of them says the readings are entries of a table, that the table has sixteen of them, that eight settings share one, that the two mid sections share it, or that the entries are the third octaves the page's two ends bracket. That is the whole of what is added here, and it is added by holding five candidate laws against the same readings rather than by fitting one to them.

Either rotor's rate differing between the two types by more than a cent at any setting out of transit -- from value 16 upward on a low rotor and 17 on a high one, under any state both types can be put in.

Every effect parameter this unit powers up holding is a value its own manual prints as that parameter's default. 575 parameters across sixty-five types were in a position to disagree and none did, 154 of them at a byte the printing leaves no choice about.

Four printed parameters had no claim within reach of them by any reading of the coverage, and this is the first measurement of any of them. It also puts a second byte on the placement class's records without a take being made: the azimuth sweep was run twice and the second run has been sitting beside the first as a control rather than as evidence about its own byte.

Nothing structural had been read on this type at all. What the archive held of these two bytes was two rate records, one per byte, each taken with the other byte at what the type powers it up holding -- and neither is a reading of the byte it swept. The first is not monotonic across the printed table and the second does not move with its byte at all. This says what those two records are readings of, which is the pair, and it says which of the two bytes is the quantity and which is the clock. It also says what parks this type, which no run of it had: the bottom of the printed table is a modulator that does not turn inside a take, and it is the only parking either byte offers.

Nothing structural had been read on this type. The archive held no reading of either pitch byte and none of the mode byte, whose page prints five numbered states and no unit at all -- so what the number counted was not merely unknown, it had no candidate quantity. This says what it is the length of, and it says it in the unit the rest of this machine's delays are already measured in. It also supplies the one thing a pitch byte's own sweep cannot: a null. A shifter asked for no shift produces no splice, so the setting at the middle of both bytes is the run's own control and it sits inside the sweep rather than beside it.

One parameter powering up on a byte its page prints no default at, where the page marks a default and the conversion pins it to a single byte. Those are where this claim is at risk; the rest sit inside a run of bytes the page prints one setting across, and could have agreed by landing anywhere in it.

The archive says what each byte did to each band. It does not say that those profiles are the response of a cascade of second-order sections, that the low shelf is one pole rather than two, or that the two mids are one law rather than two that happen to agree at the three settings both were asked at. Each of those is a structure fitted to the readings, and the fit is what this file holds.

The archive says what the manual byte did to each third-octave band at nine settings. It does not say those profiles are the magnitude of a phase -- that the dips are cancellations between a signal and a delayed-in-phase copy of itself rather than filters with stopbands, that there are eight sections rather than six or ten, that the dry and wet are summed rather than averaged, or that the chain runs at thirty-two kilohertz. Each is a structure fitted to the readings, and the fit is what this holds.

The byte a 3D type prints `Speaker/Phones` against does not switch an output on or off and does not change a level. It picks between two renderings of the same placement, and which rendering is in use changes how the two channels are separated as a function of frequency. On the median plane the two renderings are the same thing: at the front and directly behind, where the placement leaves the two channels level, every one of a hundred and thirteen twelfth octaves agrees to within two tenths of a decibel and so does the total. Everywhere else they differ, and the difference turns over with frequency -- the speaker rendering separates the channels more below a hundred and twenty five hertz and less above two kilohertz, at 24 of the 24 placements that can show it -- every one of them -- and by up to 13.8 decibels in a band. The speaker rendering is also about a decibel and a half louder over the two channels together. The whole of it is antisymmetric about the front: the placement on one side returns the negative of its mirror to within 2.6 dB at the worst of 15 pairs, which is what says this is a property of the byte and the placement rather than of the takes. The same four are returned by the other type that places by a byte, read after the placement it names has arrived, so this is what the stage does and not what one type does.

The byte a page prints `Drive` against sets how hard a signal is driven into a fixed nonlinearity. It does not choose between curves and it does not change the curve: over the settings the comparison can reach, feeding the stage a louder signal at one drive returns the same reading as raising the drive at one input, the reading being the level at each whole multiple of the carrier under the level at the carrier. That is a statement about the stage and not about the signal. If the stage is one curve behind one gain then scaling what it is fed has the same effect whatever it is fed, so all this needs is that both sides of every comparison were made on the same signal, which they were. It is worth saying what it therefore does not need, because the signal is not what the run took it for: the voice is two oscillators about twelve cents apart at nearly the same size, so it beats, and the stage was driven at a level that moved through each take rather than one that stood still. The correspondence survives that untouched. What is read at each multiple of the carrier does not, and nothing here is a harmonic series. The input each setting wants is what that setting's own value gives when it is read as a gain -- twenty times the log of it over 48, in decibels, and 48 is where the page rests the byte rather than an origin chosen here. From setting 8 to 48 the wanted input tracks that law to between a tenth and four tenths of a decibel, against bars of a tenth to four and four tenths that the ladder measures for itself by putting each of its own rungs back from the others. The tightest of those rows is setting 32, where the law is asked to a tenth of a decibel and answers to a tenth. Two bounds, both measured. The byte's bottom three settings return one state -- 0, 2 and 4 agree order for order inside the run's own repeats -- so whatever the byte is there it is not a gain, which would have to be three different ones. Above 48 every setting wants more input than the part can give, and the comparison says nothing about them rather than pinning them to the ladder's last rung. The other standalone drive type is a different curve and not the same one rested somewhere else. No state this type can be put in comes within seven and nine tenths of a decibel of any state of that one, against repeats that agree to two hundredths. What the stage is fed is not the carrier: a fixed filter stands in front of it, and what reaches the curve is a shaped version. The stage's small-signal gain at the carrier is 11.87 decibels at 110 hertz, 20.37 at 220 and 23.08 at 330 -- a tilt of 11.21 decibels, 8.50 of it in the first octave. The level the three were fed is one level: across all 10 rungs of the ladder the three carriers differ in what went into the stage by at most 0.10 of a decibel, which is the worst of the rungs and not a chosen one. And where the ladder stops moving the output, the carrier comes to rest at -39.84, -39.93 and -40.49 decibels -- a spread of 0.65, against a tilt of 11.21 going in. A filter after the curve would carry that tilt onto the ceiling, because a curve that limits puts out what it puts out and anything after it multiplies that; a filter in front changes only how much arrives, so three carriers rest at one level however differently they got there. The ceiling is flat and the gain is not, so the tilt is in front. None of this moves the law above. Feeding one carrier a louder signal at one drive still matches raising the drive at one input, because the filter is the same filter on both sides of every comparison and every comparison was made on one carrier. What it does move is what the curve is taken to be fed: the input a setting wants is the input at the part, and the input at the curve is that input through a filter nobody here has identified. Its shape is not read off these three points -- eight and a half decibels in the first octave is steeper than any one-pole can be, and that is the whole of what the spacing supports. The tilt is a floor rather than a figure, and errs the safe way: the gain at the lowest carrier is the same at the bottom three rungs and is therefore the small-signal one, while at the highest carrier the gain is already falling by the second rung, so the number read there is under that carrier's own small-signal gain and the distance between them is under the true distance.

**The curve does not run out of orders, and near zero it is not smooth.** The byte was swept again on the voice measured to be one component at this note, read to 32 orders, and the series was asked how it behaves high up. At the setting the page rests the type at, the odd orders fall 6.3 decibels an order from the 11th to the 23rd and then stop falling: from the 25th to the 31st they sit at -77 decibels under the first, where the rate the low orders set would have carried them to -109. What is there stands 31 decibels over that, 37 over the same order of the take routed past the effect, and 72 over the floor between the orders in its own take -- so it is neither the voice, nor the chain, nor a floor the reading is sitting on. Across those last four odd orders the series falls 2.6 decibels, which is a power of the order and not an exponential: a curve smooth on the scale of the signal loses its orders faster than any power, and that is the whole of what the two readings differed by. Which power is not settled here. A jump gives 1.9 decibels across these four orders and a kink in the slope gives 3.7, and the repeats of one setting in this record fail to agree by more than the difference between them. A step and a corner are both what the smooth reading was not, and telling them apart is a finer question than the one that was asked.

**Read at one setting of the byte and not across it.** What stands over a high order is what this same stage makes of the voice's other partials, which is bounded by driving a stand-in curve as hard as the unit is driven. Below the resting place the stand-in cannot be brought near the unit's low orders at all -- 11 decibels away at the worst -- so the bound it returns is a number about the stand-in. Above it the low orders match and the drive that matches them is hard enough that the stand-in's own high orders stand over everything the unit shows, which is a bound that admits nothing rather than a reading that failed. One setting is what this run reads, and it is the one the page rests the type at.

The byte a page prints `Small/BltIn/2-Stk/3-Stk` against is one table of four fixed responses, written once and reached from more than one place, and it sits after the drive stage rather than shaping what goes into it. One table, because an entry read on a type that is nothing but a drive stage and the same entry read from inside a pair land a median 0.18 dB apart across a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands, where the same reading puts two different entries of the table 1.96 dB apart or more -- so the reading separates the entries by better than an order of magnitude over what it says separates these. After the drive stage, because the pair was read once with each of the two drive characters its selector offers, and those characters put out measurably different spectra: a median 3.87 dB apart in shape and 9.99 dB at their widest, one carrying nine decibels more above eight kilohertz and the other seven more through the midrange. A filter shaping the input to a nonlinearity does not divide out of the result, because the nonlinearity remaps whatever spectrum it is given; a filter after one does, exactly. The ratio between two amp entries is 0.09 dB apart between the two characters, which is under the runs' own repeats -- so it divides out, and the filter is on the output. The switch beside the byte is what puts the table in the path at all: at Off the profile is its own reference to a median of a seventh of a decibel, and at On it is a bandpass, 10.7 dB down through the bottom octave and 3.2 down above eight kilohertz against 4.9 up through the two to four kilohertz octave. Read in five more places the table holds and in a sixth it does not. The bass multi-effect is the one place that does not reach it. Driving the stage at 4 and at 127 rather than the 48 the first run held moves each entry's response by a median 0.165 and 0.18 dB -- a thirty-two-fold change in the drive byte, against a reading that puts two entries of the table 2.3 dB apart. The two families the first run could not reach return the same four as well: the stage followed by a chorus at 0.2 dB and the same stage as one of five in a guitar chain at 0.22, both at the same three entries and on the same band set. So one table is reached from three families, two printed shapes, at three different parameter numbers, and at three drive amounts spanning almost the whole byte. The bass multi is the exception and it is not a close one: its first three entries sit a median 7.7 dB from the same three read anywhere else, which is wider than the table's own entries are from each other, and its fourth setting -- the one its row prints no name against -- returns its reference to 0.13 dB while sitting 7.81 dB from the entry below it. Not the third entry repeated, not the fourth the other rows return, and not refused: the first entry, which is what the byte would give if its top value did not reach the table. The bass type was then asked which side of its own drive stage it sits on. Its own table sits after its own stage, so this unit has two of them and not one. Its entries move by a median 0.13 dB when the drive byte goes to 4 and 0.24 when it goes to 127, against its own entries sitting 6.41 dB from each other -- 27 times the larger of the two. So the one type that reaches different curves reaches them the same way the other five do, and the reading that would have made the disagreement an artefact of where the filter sits is refused. What is left is the plainest arrangement and not the cheapest one: two tables, one of four responses for the guitar-side types and one for the bass, each written after the nonlinearity it is heard through.

The byte a page prints `Threshold` against is decibels, 0.4776 of them a step over two independent twenty-one step stretches that agree to 0.0009, and the limiting stops at byte 61.2 for the level this was read at, above which the four states of the ratio byte are one reading to 0.01 of a decibel. The type takes a further 2.7 decibels off whatever it is doing, constant across thirty decibels of input and therefore not limiting. Of the four states of the byte printed `Ratio`, only the one printed `1/100` behaves as a ratio: its gain reduction is proportional to how far the signal sits over the threshold to a part in a thousand. The other three do not. What that sentence is about is their gain reduction being proportional to the distance over the threshold, which is a different quantity from the slope: each of the three still takes six to eight and a half tenths of a decibel off where the signal sits at the threshold, so the line it follows does not pass through the threshold. Walked as a ladder instead -- the level going in moved thirty-six decibels at one setting of the threshold byte, which uses no part of that byte -- each of the four states returns a slope, and one minus that slope comes back 0.2499, 0.5052, 0.7518 and 0.9947: a quarter, a half, three quarters and all of the level over the threshold, to within a part in a hundred. The page names the middle two of those correctly and the outer two not. The state printed `1/1.5` takes three quarters of the level away where two thirds is printed against it, and the state printed `1/100` holds its output still to a hundredth of a decibel over eight decibels of input, where one part in a hundred would have moved it eight times the run's own floor. Four fixed ratios of one quantity make the gain reductions a rank one table, whose columns would stand in one proportion; measured, that proportion walks from 1.682 to 1.523 across the four states, and the ratio each of the three returns changes with how far over the threshold it is asked.

The byte beside this type's manual is the gain of a feedback loop closed around the all-pass cascade, and it is not a second mix and not a resonance inside the sections. A cascade passes everything at unit gain, so summing it with the dry signal reaches six decibels where the two arrive in phase and no further; the profile reaches 18.87 dB, which a sum would need nearly eight helpings of the cascade to do. What the loop puts there instead is a resonance between each pair of notches -- where the cascade comes back in phase with itself and the return adds up -- while the notches stay where the closed reading put them. Two further things about it are readable, one at each end of the band. The return arrives one sample late, which is what a part computing a sample at a time has no choice about, and the phase that costs is nothing at the bottom and half a circle at half the rate: at the top of the band it turns the highest resonance into the cancellation it would otherwise have been, which the unit does and an instantaneous loop does not. And the return will not carry the bottom of the band: the lowest resonance is largest at 105 Hz and has fallen thirteen decibels by 25, by more the harder the loop is driven and by nothing at all when the loop is open -- which puts one pole of a high pass inside the loop and nowhere else in the chain. The loop gains themselves are a readout of seventeen settings and no law is claimed on them. What the seventeen do settle is that there is something to claim: the gain moves at every one of them, and the two that share the top four bits of the byte come back 0.0675 apart -- further than any neighbouring pair of the sweep -- so this byte is not the sixteen-entry table the byte one address along on the same type turned out to be.

The byte printed `Lo-Fi Type 1 - 6 - 9` at `40 03 04` on type `01 72` is not one quantity with nine values. It is two fields of one byte, and the two are told apart by where they show rather than by any arithmetic on the index.

**What the low field does is hold the signal for a whole number of samples.** Read with the type's own filters parked where they were measured to pass the most, the nine entries are three behaviours each appearing three times, grouped by the index modulo three: inside a group the profiles agree to 0.34 dB at the median against a floor of 0.25 dB, and the nearest two entries from different groups differ by 0.66 dB. One group is flat. The second puts a null 19 dB deep at 10679 Hz and the third one 26 dB deep at 8000 Hz, and all three entries of each group put it in the same band. A null is what holding a sample for a whole number of periods does and a low pass table is not: the third group's profile comes back up after its null and goes down again at the top of the band set, which is a second null where a hold of four samples has to have one and where nothing with one corner does.

**And the two nulls measure the rate rather than assuming it.** They stand in the ratio 1.3348, which is 5.0 bands of this set apart and is four to three to inside one of them. Read as a hold of three samples and a hold of four, they imply a rate of 32036 Hz and 32000 Hz -- two numbers this record produces independently of each other, agreeing to a tenth of a per cent, and agreeing with the 32000 Hz this archive reads on classes that share none of these takes.

The part of the difference that depends on the setting is 0.13 dB at the median and runs between thirteen and forty-two times under what the byte commands at that same setting. The record says how loud the take was at each of the hundred and twenty-eight settings, and says in as many words that no law, no curve and no quantum is in it. The high side has been read twice since -- once through a shelf whose half-gain point is where its parameter says it is, and once on a grid 25 times finer than the one that found it -- and it comes back 6872 to 7240 Hz, a band of 5.4 per cent shared by the five records whose own floors close on it. It is far narrower than it was and it is still a range. The two corners the model carries sit inside those ranges and are kept, because nothing measured moves them and a second point estimate would be the same artefact with a different value. What the agreement between types is worth is that no type's range sits outside the others' -- which is what was being asked, and is now asked of six.

The two bytes had no claim on them and neither had ever been read, though the takes for both have been published since the degrader beside them was closed. What is new is the structure inside each table -- a ladder with a switch for one, a shelf table for the other -- and the measurement that they are not one table.

The two pre-filters departing at a setting neither run asked -- the grid is eleven of a hundred and twenty-eight through the low pass and four through the high pass, so a table that agreed at those and not between them would look exactly like this. Or either type's filter turning out to move with something the other's does not: both runs parked the modulator and opened the loop, and a pre-filter that depended on either would have been read at one point of a surface rather than as a curve.

The two records say what this byte did to each twelfth-octave band at three settings, once with the type's mix at the top of its range and once at its middle. What is read out of them here is that the byte is a loop rather than a mix or a section resonance, where the loop is closed, that its return is a sample late, and that it does not pass the bottom of the band. The two renderings coming back identical at a placement off the median plane, or differing at the front. This type is a chain of four fixed filter sections and an output gain: a low shelf, two peaking sections that share one law, a high shelf. The low shelf is one pole and one zero, and so is the high one -- which the band profiles this was read from could not say, because they are magnitude and a second-order section differs from a first-order one in phase everywhere and in magnitude only past a corner this unit has no output beyond. Each parameter byte selects from a short table rather than driving a formula -- a gain answers over twenty-five values and sticks at both ends, a corner has two states, a width has five entries and returns the first for anything past them, a centre moves in equal steps of log frequency for every eighth value of its byte, at the named third octaves between the printed ends and at one entry that is not one of them.

This type is eight first-order all-pass sections in series, summed with the dry signal rather than averaged with it, running at thirty-two kilohertz. One byte moves every section's corner together, which puts four cancellations in the audible band at fixed ratios read in the tangent of frequency -- so they crowd towards each other in hertz as the byte takes them up, and the top ones leave the band rather than staying four.

This type is eight peaking sections parked at fixed centres, one output pan and one level, with a single width byte driving all eight instead of one each. The centres are the named third octaves at 250, 500, 1k, 1.25k, 2k, 3.15k, 4k and 8k: a band raised to the top of its byte and cut to the bottom returns the same centre to within 0.02 octaves, and the eight sit 0.030 octaves under the named series with a scatter of 0.018 -- which is the offset this unit's other equaliser's table was measured to carry. Two settings inside one of these entries returning frequencies the run tells apart, or two settings across an entry boundary returning frequencies it does not. Type `01 60`'s pitch bytes are not read by anything that runs at a rate of its own. They are read out of a window, and the output repeats every time the read-out has drifted that window's length -- so the rate a take carries is `|r - 1| / T`, where `r` is the ratio the two pitch bytes ask for and `T` is the window. Across the coarse byte the ratio was moved from a quarter to double, which is `|r - 1|` from 0.056 to 1.000, and the rate moved with it from 0.90 to 15.63 Hz: over that factor of eighteen `T` stays between 62.1 and 64.7 ms. At unison the line is not slow, it is gone -- byte 64 returns 4.81 Hz, which is this voice's own amplitude wobble and the same figure the fine byte returns at its own unison. On the fine byte, which reaches ratios three orders closer to one than the coarse byte's smallest step does, the four settings whose implied rate clears the run's own floor of 0.3033 Hz come back at 0.4504 to 0.9384 Hz and give `T` of 63.21 to 63.74 ms, while every setting between them returns the voice's wobble instead -- which is what a window rate under the floor looks like and is not something a clock of the stage's own could do. The byte the page prints `Shift Mode` against, over five states and with no unit beside them, moves `T` and moves nothing else. Its five states return 32.00, 42.68, 63.78, 85.27 and 128.0 ms, which is the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12, read at two shifts an octave apart. The shortest is 1024 steps of the 32000 Hz clock this archive already reads this unit's delay ladder as cut to; the third is 2048 of them and the fifth is 4096, so three of the five are successive powers of two and the two between them sit a fourth and a fifth along -- two octaves reached in four steps. Read at the octave, where the two shortest windows put the rate past the 20 Hz ceiling this reading searches to, those two and only those two come back at exactly half: 15.6261 where 31.25 is asked for, and 11.7221 where 23.44 is.

Type `01 61`'s mode byte picks a length, and the five it picks stand in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12 -- the ratio the single pitch shifter's five windows were measured to stand in. Read as the distance the output holds a copy of itself at, with the shifter two semitones up where four takes of one state land 0.021 ms apart, the five states give 28.505, 38.000, 57.000, 75.995 and 114.026 ms -- against the first state 1.000, 1.333, 2.000, 2.666 and 4.000 where the ratio predicts 1, 1.333, 2, 2.667 and 4, every one of them inside that 0.021. At unison the same five land up to 10.52 ms apart from themselves, five hundred times further, so the reading the ratio rests on is the shifted one and the unison takes bound nothing. Each distance is 0.8906 of the window at the same state, to four figures across all five, and that multiple is not explained here.

`Pre Filter 1 - 2 - 6` at `40 03 03` and `Post Filter 1 - 2 - 6` at `40 03 05` sit on one type, one on each side of its degrader, and are printed with the same name ending over the same range and the same six byte values. **They are two tables.**

**What the pre filter holds is a gain ladder with one stage switched across it.** Five of its six entries are three rungs 5.99 dB apart, and the rungs are gains rather than shapes: over the bands this reads they are the same number in every band to within 0.53 dB, against 0.62 dB from the same six entries swept twice in two sessions, and they tilt by 0.04 dB per octave at worst over six of them. The odd entries carry one stage and the even entries carry it with something else added, and the something else is the same curve both times: the step from entry one to entry two and the step from entry three to entry four agree to 0.16 dB at the median and 0.69 dB at worst. Entry nought is not a fourth rung: it stands 17.13 dB under entry one with a spread of 1.76 dB and a tilt of -0.27 dB per octave, both outside what the floor produces, so it is a different shape and not the bottom of the ladder.

**And what that stage is, is a notch and not a low pass.** It falls to -8.20 dB at 8000 Hz and comes back to nothing above it, reaching a quarter of a decibel of flat again by fifteen kilohertz -- which a corner cannot do and a dip in the middle of the band can. Fitted as a second order notch with its centre, its sharpness and its depth all free, the centre lands at 8000 Hz (Q 0.42, 0.61 of the way to a full null, residual 0.146 dB), and moving the centre five hundred hertz either way more than doubles that residual. **That stage is one tap added at two samples.** Held out a half of the band set at a time, the tap predicts the bands it was not shown to 0.44 and 0.31 dB while the freely centred section misses them by 2.33 and 3.25 -- and the section's centre lands at 9300 Hz from one half and 5550 Hz from the other, so the range as a whole is what was placing it. Rendering both through the band energies the unit was read as, rather than sampling them at the band centres, moves either curve by at most 0.042 dB and changes nothing. **8000 Hz is a quarter of 32000 Hz**, which is the clock this archive reads on classes that share no takes with these -- a delay ladder, a degrader's own two nulls -- and which nothing in this fit was told.

**What the post filter holds is not that.** The same three rungs, asked the same way, are shapes and not gains: they spread 2.90 to 2.96 dB where the pre filter's spread 0.31 to 0.53. The same alternation is there and its stage agrees with itself just as well (0.20 dB), but it is a different stage: deepest at 132 Hz where the pre filter's is deepest at 8000 Hz, with nothing below it coming back, and the two differ from each other by 5.28 dB at the median against a floor of 0.15. The entry that passes the most is the last of one byte and the first of the other.

**So a rule closed on one of them does not reach the other**, and the two are indistinguishable to anything reading the printed page: same last word, same range, same hex values, same type.
